rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit ban on killing a protected soul reiterates a prohibition already included in the ban on manifest and hidden abominations.
rows.anchor: وهذا مما نص تبارك وتعالى على النهي عنه تأكيدا، وإلا فهو داخل في النهي عن الفواحش ما ظهر منها وما بطن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The Prophet limits lawful Muslim blood to three cases: a married adulterer, a life taken in retaliation, or one who abandons religion and the community; Ibn Kathir cites the report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود، رضي الله عنه، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A Muslim's blood is lawful only for a married adulterer to be stoned, an intentional killer to be killed, or an apostate who wages war against God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة، رضي الله عنها؛ أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
rows.claim: While besieged, Uthman invokes a Prophetic report listing apostasy, adultery after marriage, and killing as the only grounds for Muslim blood, asserts his innocence of all three, and is killed unjustly; al-Tirmidhi grades it ḥasan.
rows.anchor: وقال الترمذي: هذا حديث حسن

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The Prophet warns that killing a treaty-protected non-Muslim bars the killer from even smelling Paradise, whose scent reaches forty years' distance.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو، رضي الله عنهما، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet warns that one who violates God’s and His Messenger’s covenant with a protected person will not smell Paradise, whose scent reaches seventy autumns away.
rows.anchor: فلا يرح رائحة الجنة، وإن ريحها ليوجد من مسيرة سبعين خريفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's injunctions are given so people may understand and heed His commands and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: لعلكم تعقلون عنه أمره ونهيه.

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The report is transmitted by Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhi, who grade it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: رواه ابن ماجه، والترمذي وقال: حسن صحيح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After the orphan-property warning, caretakers separated the orphan's food and drink, but leftovers spoiled; the Prophet then received 2:220 permitting shared food and drink when managing orphans is for their good. Reported by Abū Dāwūd.
rows.anchor: فانطلق من كان عنده يتيم فعزل طعامه من طعامه وشرابه من شرابه

rows.speaker: الشعبي ومالك وغير واحد من السلف
rows.claim: The orphan reaches full maturity at puberty.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي، ومالك، وغير واحد من السلف: يعني: حتى يحتلم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī places the age of full maturity at thirty; other views say forty or sixty, which Ibn Kathīr judges remote in this context.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: حتى يبلغ ثلاثين سنة، وقيل: أربعون سنة، وقيل: ستون سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed ages of thirty, forty, and sixty are all far-fetched for the maturity meant here.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله بعيد هاهنا، والله أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fair dealing requires justice in both taking and giving; God threatened people who short measure or weight and destroyed a nation for cheating with measures and scales.
rows.anchor: يأمر تعالى بإقامة العدل في الأخذ والإعطاء، كما توعد على تركه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet warns those responsible for measuring and weighing that earlier nations perished through this responsibility; al-Tirmidhi says the raised report is known only through al-Ḥusayn ibn Qays, who is weak, while a sound version stops at Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: ثم قال: لا نعرفه مرفوعا إلا من حديث الحسين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report says the community entrusted with measuring and weighing was given the two practices by which earlier generations perished.
rows.anchor: إنكم معشر الموالي قد بشركم الله بخصلتين بها هلكت القرون المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever makes a full effort to give and receive what is due is not blameworthy for an error after exhausting their ability.
rows.anchor: من اجتهد في أداء الحق وأخذه، فإن أخطأ بعد استفراغ وسعه وبذل جهده فلا حرج عليه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: A person who measures and weighs fully with sincere intent is not held accountable; Ibn Kathīr calls this a rare disconnected report.
rows.anchor: وذلك تأويل {وسعها} هذا مرسل غريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech and action alike must be just toward relatives and strangers, at every time and in every circumstance.
rows.anchor: يأمر تعالى بالعدل في الفعال والمقال، على القريب والبعيد

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Fulfilling God's covenant means obeying what He commands and forbids and acting by His Book and the Messenger's Sunnah.
rows.anchor: أن تطيعوه فيما أمركم ونهاكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The injunctions are emphasized so people may take heed and stop their former conduct; some recite the ذال in تذكرون with doubling and others without it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعضهم بتشديد "الذال"، وآخرون بتخفيفها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: God commands believers to remain united and forbids disagreement and division in religion; Mujāhid and others say earlier peoples perished through religious disputation and quarrels.
rows.anchor: أمر الله المؤمنين بالجماعة، ونهاهم عن الاختلاف والفرقة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The Prophet drew one straight line as God's path and side lines as other paths, each with a devil calling to it; al-Ḥākim calls the chain sound.
rows.anchor: هذه السبل ليس منها سبيل إلا عليه شيطان يدعو إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥākim authenticates the Ibn Masʿūd report through both routes; Ibn Kathīr suggests ʿĀṣim may have heard it from both Zur and Abū Wāʾil, each from Ibn Masʿūd.
rows.anchor: ولعل هذا الحديث عند عاصم بن أبي النجود، عن زر، وعن أبي وائل شقيق بن سلمة كلاهما عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: A supporting report depicts the straight path with the Prophet's line and the devil's paths on either side; al-Ḥākim says its route from al-Shaʿbī is not dependable.
rows.anchor: وشاهد هذا الحديث حديث الشعبي عن جابر، من وجه غير معتمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn Masʿūd report is the main authority despite possible consequential variation, and it may also have been transmitted as Ibn Masʿūd's own statement.
rows.anchor: ولكن العمدة على حديث ابن مسعود، مع ما فيه من الاختلاف إن كان مؤثرا، وقد روي موقوفا عليه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Asked about the straight path, Ibn Masʿūd describes a route ending in Paradise flanked by side roads with callers; those taking the side roads end in Hell, while the straight route ends in Paradise.
rows.anchor: تركنا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم في أدناه، وطرفه في الجنة

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: The Prophet's parable identifies the straight path as Islam, its walls as God's limits, open doors as forbidden things, the caller at its head as God's Book, and the inner caller as God's counsel in each Muslim heart; al-Tirmidhi grades it ḥasan gharīb.
rows.anchor: فالصراط الإسلام، والسوران حدود الله، والأبواب المفتحة محارم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's path is singular because truth is one, while the other paths are plural because they divide and branch; the contrast is like believers being brought from darkness into light.
rows.anchor: الحق واحد؛ ولهذا جمع لتفرقها وتشعبها

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: The Prophet sought a pledge to uphold the three verses beginning 6:151: fulfillment earns God's reward; violation may be punished in this life or left to God's choice in the next.
rows.anchor: ومن وفى بهن أجره على الله، ومن انتقص منهن شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh accuses the magicians of conspiring with Moses to seize power, expel the leaders, and control the city, then says they will see what he does to them.
rows.anchor: أي: تجتمعوا أنتم وهو، وتكون لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh threatens to cut each person's opposite hand and foot and crucify them all; the parallel wording says they would be crucified on palm trunks.
rows.anchor: يعني: يقطع يد الرجل اليمنى ورجله اليسرى أو بالعكس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Pharaoh was the first to crucify people and to cut hands and feet on opposite sides.
rows.anchor: أول من صلب، وأول من قطع الأيدي والأرجل من خلاف، فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians know they will return to God, whose punishment is harsher than Pharaoh's; they will endure Pharaoh's torture to escape God's punishment and seek steadfastness in Moses' religion.
rows.anchor: قد تحققنا أنا إليه راجعون، وعذابه أشد من عذابك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعبيد بن عمير وقتادة وابن جريج
rows.claim: The magicians were sorcerers in the morning and steadfast martyrs by evening after asking for patience and death as Muslims.
rows.anchor: كانوا في أول النهار سحرة، وفي آخره شهداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A polytheist seeking protection must be allowed to hear the Quran and a proof of the religion, then remain safe until escorted home; this lets the uninformed learn God's religion and lets His call spread.
rows.anchor: ليعلموا دين الله، وتنتشر دعوة الله في عباده

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Any person who comes to hear what the Prophet says and what has been revealed is safe until hearing it and reaching the place from which he came.
rows.anchor: إنسان يأتيك يسمع ما تقول وما أنزل عليك، فهو آمن حتى يأتيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet gave safe passage to Quraysh envoys at Ḥudaybiyyah, including ʿUrwa, Makraz, and Suhayl; impressed by Muslim reverence for him, they reported it at home and helped lead many to Islam.
rows.anchor: فرأوا من إعظام المسلمين رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما بهرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger of Musaylimah affirmed his master's claim, so the Prophet said he would have beheaded him if envoys were killed; Ibn Masʿūd later executed him after he publicly endorsed Musaylimah outside a mission.
rows.anchor: لولا أن الرسل لا تقتل لضربت عنقك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A visitor from enemy territory for a message, trade, peace, truce, tribute, or similar purpose receives protection until returning home; scholars disallow a full-year stay, permit four months, and differ on the interval between.
rows.anchor: فطلب من الإمام أو نائبه أمانا، أعطي أمانا ما دام مترددا في دار الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rainwater makes crops grow by God's power, as illustrated by the listed produce; the question about who provides it invokes 80:27–31 and 67:21 to establish His exclusive lordship.
rows.anchor: من ذا الذي ينزل من السماء ماء المطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave people hearing and sight and could take them away; Ibn Kathīr links this to 67:23 and 6:46.
rows.anchor: الذي وهبكم هذه القوة السامعة، والقوة الباصرة، ولو شاء لذهب بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bringing the living from the dead and the dead from the living occurs by God's immense power and grace; the verse is general and includes all the interpretations previously discussed.
rows.anchor: بقدرته العظيمة، ومنته العميمة، وقد تقدم ذكر الخلاف في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone governs all creation and none can overturn His judgment; every heavenly and earthly creature depends on Him, as in 55:29.
rows.anchor: وهو المتصرف الحاكم الذي لا معقب لحكمه، ولا يسأل عما يفعل وهم يسألون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the polytheists admit God does all this, they should fear Him instead of worshiping others through opinion and ignorance.
rows.anchor: أفلا تخافون منه أن تعبدوا معه غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Creator and controller whom they acknowledge is the true Lord worthy of exclusive worship; every other object of worship is false.
rows.anchor: فكل معبود سواه باطل، لا إله إلا هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who know God created, provides for, and governs everything are asked how they can turn from worshiping Him to worshiping anything else.
rows.anchor: عن عبادته إلى عبادة ما سواه، وأنتم تعلمون أنه الرب الذي خلق كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists persist in associating partners with God despite acknowledging His sole creative and governing power, so His decree makes them destined for misery in Hell, as in 39:71.
rows.anchor: حقت عليهم كلمة الله أنهم أشقياء من ساكني النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers lose themselves in blazing Hell and their invented gods disappear, failing to help and instead harming them; other verses show their former idols disowning them.
rows.anchor: أي: خسروا أنفسهم لأنهم دخلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are the greatest losers in the afterlife, trading the heights of Paradise and its delights for Hell's depths and punishments, and God's nearness and vision for His anger.
rows.anchor: استبدلوا بالدركات عن الدرجات، واعتاضوا عن نعيم الجنان بحميم آن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After abandoning Joseph in the well, his brothers return to Jacob at night pretending grief and explain that they left him with their belongings while they raced and a wolf ate him.
rows.anchor: رجعوا إلى أبيهم في ظلمة الليل يبكون، ويظهرون الأسف والجزع على يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their claim that Jacob would not believe them even if truthful is calculated tact: they acknowledge his suspicion was understandable because he had warned them about the wolf and the outcome sounds unlikely.
rows.anchor: تلطف عظيم في تقرير ما يحاولونه، يقولون: ونحن نعلم أنك لا تصدقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers used fabricated blood to reinforce their plot, slaughtering a young lamb and smearing Joseph's shirt but forgetting to tear it; Jacob sees through their scheme and commits to beautiful patience and God's help against their lies.
rows.anchor: فذبحوها، ولطخوا ثوب يوسف بدمها، موهمين أن هذا قميصه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and others infer that a wolf would have torn the shirt if it had eaten Joseph.
rows.anchor: قال: لو أكله السبع لخرق القميص

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Beautiful patience is patience without distress or agitation.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: الصبر الجميل: الذي لا جزع فيه

rows.speaker: حبان بن أبي جبلة
rows.claim: A disconnected report attributes to the Prophet the definition of beautiful patience as patience without complaint.
rows.anchor: وهذا مرسل

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: A saying attributed by al-Thawrī to one of his companions lists three forms of patience: do not mention your pain, misfortune, or praise yourself.
rows.anchor: ثلاث من الصبر: ألا تحدث بوجعك، ولا بمصيبتك، ولا تزكي نفسك

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: During the slander incident, ʿĀʾishah compared herself and her accusers to Joseph's father, invoking beautiful patience and God's help against what they described.
rows.anchor: والله لا أجد لي ولكم مثلا إلا أبا يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God prepared everything people need in all circumstances, whether requested by their condition or words; some early authorities include what people ask for and what they do not.
rows.anchor: يقول: هيأ لكم كل ما تحتاجون إليه في جميع أحوالكم

rows.speaker: بعض السلف
rows.claim: God gives people everything they ask for and what they do not ask for.
rows.anchor: من كل ما سألتموه وما لم تسألوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has أتاكم rather than آتاكم.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعضهم: "وأتاكم من كل ما سألتموه"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot count God's blessings, much less fulfill their duty of thanks; Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb says God's due exceeds human ability and His blessings exceed counting, so believers should repent morning and evening.
rows.anchor: ولكن أصبحوا توابين وامسوا توابين

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet praised God as the Lord who needs no provision or replacement and from whom none can dispense; the report is in al-Bukhārī.
rows.anchor: لك الحمد غير مكفي ولا مودع، ولا مستغنى عنه ربنا

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A rare, weak-chain report pictures three ledgers at Resurrection: deeds, sins, and blessings; a single blessing consumes all good deeds before God forgives and grants His mercy.
rows.anchor: غريب، وسنده ضعيف. وقد روي في الأثر

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: David asks how he can thank God when the very ability to thank is itself a gift; God says that recognizing the inability to repay blessings is now gratitude.
rows.anchor: الآن شكرتني يا داود، أي: حين اعترفت بالتقصير عن أداء شكر النعم

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says every act of thanking one blessing requires a new blessing, for which one must again give thanks.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي لا يؤدى شكر نعمة من نعمه

rows.speaker: القائل
rows.claim: A poet says that even if every limb had a tongue to praise God for His gifts, such praise would still not increase the poet's gratitude enough.
rows.anchor: لو كل جارحة مني لها لغة … تثني عليك بما أوليت من حسن

rows.speaker: القائل
rows.claim: The poem continues that even gratitude expressed through every limb cannot adequately match God's beneficence and gifts.
rows.anchor: لكان ما زاد شكري إذ شكرت به … إليك أبلغ في الإحسان والمنن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These people denied God's worldly signs and proofs of His oneness and the truth of His messengers, and rejected the Hereafter; their works are void and their scales empty of good.
rows.anchor: لا نثقل موازينهم؛ لأنها خالية عن الخير

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says a huge, heavy man will weigh no more with God than a mosquito's wing, and recites this verse; al-Bukhārī includes it and Muslim transmits a second route.
rows.anchor: إنه ليأتي الرجل العظيم السمين

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Another report says an enormous eater and drinker will not outweigh a seed; it is transmitted by Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr.
rows.anchor: يؤتى بالرجل الأكول الشروب العظيم، فيوزن بحبة فلا يزنها

rows.speaker: بريدة
rows.claim: A report describes a Qurashī man strutting in fine clothes whom God will assign no weight on Resurrection; al-Bazzār notes its narrators Wāṣil and ʿAwn are weak and unsupported.
rows.anchor: هذا ممن لا يقيم الله له يوم القيامة وزنا

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says a huge, tall man will be brought on Resurrection and weigh less than a mosquito's wing.
rows.anchor: يؤتى يوم القيامة برجل عظيم طويل، فلا يزن عند الله جناح بعوضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After completing his sheep-tending term with his father-in-law, Moses heads toward Egypt with his wife after over ten years away; on a cold, dark, stormy night he loses the way, fails to light his flint, and sees fire on a mountain.
rows.anchor: بعد ما قضى موسى الأجل الذي كان بينه وبين صهره في رعاية الغنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses hopes to bring a flame or ember; 28:29 adds a glowing brand and warmth, indicating darkness and cold.
rows.anchor: من نار. وفي الآية الأخرى: {أو جذوة من النار}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Moses was cold with his family and had lost the road; he seeks someone to guide him, or else will bring back fire for them to kindle.
rows.anchor: من يهديني إلى الطريق. وكانوا شاتين وضلوا الطريق

rows.speaker: قتادة والسدي وإبراهيم النخعي ومغيرة بن مقسم
rows.claim: In the phrase إن كنا فاعلين, these authorities understand إن as a negation: God was not doing this.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة، والسدي، وإبراهيم النخعي، ومغيرة بن مقسم، أي: ما كنا فاعلين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says إن signals negation wherever it occurs in the Quran.
rows.anchor: كل شيء في القرآن "إن" فهو إنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God makes truth plain so it defeats and erases falsehood; the warning condemns those who claim God has a child and their false assertions.
rows.anchor: نبين الحق فيدحض الباطل؛ ولهذا قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels serve God without disdain, just as Christ and the angels are not too proud to be God's servants.
rows.anchor: لا يستكبرون عن عبادته} أي: لا يستنكفون عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of the Thicket are the people of Midian; Shuaib was their kinsman, but the Quran omits their brother from the address because they were associated with worship of the Thicket tree.
rows.anchor: هم أهل مدين على الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers mistakenly treat Midian and the people of the Thicket as separate nations, so they claim Shuaib was sent to two or even three peoples.
rows.anchor: فزعم أن شعيبا عليه السلام، بعثه الله إلى أمتين

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: A weak report says Shuaib alone among prophets was sent twice, first to Midian, destroyed by a blast, then to the Thicket people, destroyed by the cloud-day punishment.
rows.anchor: إسحاق بن بشر الكاهلي -وهو ضعيف -حدثني ابن السدي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah identifies Shuaib's people with both the people of the Well and the people of the Thicket.
rows.anchor: قوم شعيب، وقوله: {وأصحاب الأيكة}

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet calls Midian and the Thicket people two nations sent Shuaib, but Ibn Kathīr calls it strange, questions its raised attribution, and prefers that they were one community described differently.
rows.anchor: وهذا غريب، وفي رفعه نظر، والأشبه أن يكون موقوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same warning to these people to give full measure and weight as in the Midian account confirms that the two names describe one people.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنهم أمة واحدة، وصفوا في كل مقام بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They must give buyers a complete measure, neither short-changing them nor taking less than the full measure when they buy; give as they take.
rows.anchor: ولكن خذوا كما تعطون، وأعطوا كما تأخذون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qisṭās means a scale or steelyard; some say the word comes from Roman usage.
rows.anchor: والقسطاس هو: الميزان، وقيل: القبان. قال بعضهم: هو معرب من الرومية

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets straight qisṭās as justice in Roman language, while Qatādah says qisṭās means justice.
rows.anchor: القسطاس المستقيم: العدل -بالرومية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not diminish people's property or spread corruption, including by highway robbery, as in 7:86.
rows.anchor: يعني: قطع الطريق، كما في الآية الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier discussion concluded Moses completed the fuller and better of the two terms; this verse's wording may also support that conclusion.
rows.anchor: قضى أتم الأجلين وأوفاهما وأبرهما وأكملهما وأنقاهما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Moses served ten years and then another ten; Ibn Kathīr has not found this view elsewhere, though Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim cite him for it.
rows.anchor: قضى عشر سنين، وبعدها عشرا أخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses longed for his homeland and family, traveled secretly from Pharaoh with his wife and his father-in-law's sheep, and lost the road on a cold, rainy, dark night.
rows.anchor: كان موسى قد اشتاق إلى بلاده وأهله، فعزم على زيارتهم في خفية من فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He seeks news because he is lost or an ember to warm the family; the fire is on the mountain's western side to his right when facing the qiblah, in a green tree by the valley.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأنه قد أضل الطريق

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd describes the tree from which Moses was called as a fresh, green samurah tree; Ibn Kathīr calls the chain fair.
rows.anchor: عبد الله قال: رأيت الشجرة التي نودي منها موسى، عليه السلام، سمرة خضراء ترف. إسناده مقارب

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: A report from Wahb calls the tree a ʿullayq, while some People of the Book say it was an ʿawsaj.
rows.anchor: شجرة من العليق، وبعض أهل الكتاب يقول: من العوسج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who cannot practice their religion in one place are commanded to migrate to God's spacious land, where they can worship Him as required.
rows.anchor: الهجرة من البلد الذي لا يقدرون فيه على إقامة الدين، إلى أرض الله الواسعة

rows.speaker: أبو يحيى مولى الزبير بن العوام
rows.claim: The Prophet says God's land and servants belong to Him, so one should settle wherever one finds good.
rows.anchor: البلاد بلاد الله، والعباد عباد الله، فحيثما أصبت خيرا فأقم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Oppressed Muslims migrated first to Abyssinia, where the Negus sheltered them, then the Prophet and the remaining Companions migrated to Medina; death catches everyone, so obey God wherever He directs and expect the return to Him.
rows.anchor: خرجوا مهاجرين إلى أرض الحبشة، ليأمنوا، على دينهم هناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will settle faithful workers forever in high chambers beneath which flow rivers of water, wine, honey, and milk, to direct as they wish; these chambers are an excellent reward.
rows.anchor: لنسكننهم منازل عالية في الجنة تجري من تحتها الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The patient remain steadfast in faith, migrate, leave enemies and even family and kin for God's sake, and trust their Lord in religious and worldly affairs.
rows.anchor: على دينهم، وهاجروا إلى الله، ونابذوا الأعداء، وفارقوا الأهل والأقرباء

rows.speaker: أبو مالك الأشعري
rows.claim: The Prophet says God prepared transparent chambers for those who feed others, speak well, fast, and pray while people sleep.
rows.anchor: أعدها الله لمن أطعم الطعام، وأطاب الكلام، وأباح الصيام، وأقام الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trust in God applies in every circumstance, religious or worldly.
rows.anchor: في أحوالهم كلها، في دينهم ودنياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Provision is not tied to one land; migrants soon had more, better provision after becoming rulers across many regions, and God supplies even creatures unable to store food for tomorrow, as in 11:6.
rows.anchor: أن الرزق لا يختص ببقعة، بل رزقه تعالى عام لخلقه حيث كانوا وأين كانوا

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet had gone four mornings without food, warned against hoarding a year's provision through weak trust, and said he did not store money or food for the next day; Ibn Kathīr later calls the report strange and its transmitter Abū al-ʿAṭūf weak.
rows.anchor: وهذه صبح رابعة منذ لم أذق طعاما ولم أجده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report about Ibn ʿUmar is strange, and Abū al-ʿAṭūf al-Jazarī is weak.
rows.anchor: وهذا حديث غريب، وأبو العطوف الجزري ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A traditional account says raven parents leave white hatchlings until their feathers darken, while God sends tiny insects to feed them in the meantime.
rows.anchor: فيظل الفرخ فاتحا فاه يتفقد أبويه

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet praises God as provider for the young raven in its nest and healer of a broken, weakened bone.
rows.anchor: وجابر العظم الكسير المهيض

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī cites the saying Travel to be healthy and provided for.
rows.anchor: كقول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم "سافروا تصحوا وترزقوا"

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says travel to gain health and profit; another version says travel, fast, and raid to gain health and spoils. Similar wording is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās as raised and from Muʿādh as stopped at him.
rows.anchor: سافروا تربحوا، وصوموا تصحوا، واغزوا تغنموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another version advises traveling with people of means and good fortune.
rows.anchor: سافروا مع ذوي الجدود والميسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave people many examples to clarify truth, yet disbelievers call any sign false or magic, as they did the moon's splitting; even every sign would not move those condemned to disbelief, as in 10:96–97.
rows.anchor: لو رأوا أي آية كانت، سواء كانت باقتراحهم أو غيره، لا يؤمنون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should patiently endure opposition, trusting God's promised victory and good end, and stand firm because truth alone is guidance rather than being unsettled by unbelievers.
rows.anchor: بل اثبت على ما بعثك الله به، فإنه الحق الذي لا مرية فيه

rows.speaker: صحابي من أصحاب النبي
rows.claim: When the Prophet stumbled while reciting Sūrat al-Rūm in dawn prayer, he said poor ablution by some worshipers had confused the Quran and instructed those praying with him to perform ablution well; Ibn Kathīr grades the chain and text ḥasan and infers the follower's prayer is connected to the imam's.
rows.anchor: وهذا إسناد حسن ومتن حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman, whom God honored for wisdom, advises his beloved son first to worship God alone and warns that associating partners with Him is the greatest injustice; the son is named Tharan in a report cited by al-Suhaylī.
rows.anchor: فهو حقيق أن يمنحه أفضل ما يعرف؛ ولهذا أوصاه أولا بأن يعبد الله وحده

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: When 6:82 troubled the Companions because they thought it condemned all wrongdoing, the Prophet explained that it meant shirk, citing Luqman's saying that shirk is a great injustice; Bukhārī and Muslim transmit it.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "أنه ليس بذاك، ألا (3) تسمع إلى قول لقمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship of God alone is paired with kindness to parents, as in 17:23 and often elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: وكثيرا ما يقرن تعالى بين ذلك في القرآن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets the mother's weakness upon weakness as the hardship of carrying her child; Qatādah says strain upon strain and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says weakness upon weakness.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: مشقة وهن الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Weaning in two years means the child's rearing and nursing after birth; this matches 2:233.
rows.anchor: تربيته وإرضاعه بعد وضعه في عامين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and other imams infer a minimum pregnancy of six months by comparing thirty months for pregnancy and weaning in 46:15 with a full two-year nursing term.
rows.anchor: أن أقل مدة الحمل ستة أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mention of the mother's toil, including nights awake, recalls her prior care and calls the child to show her kindness, as in 17:24; God will richly reward gratitude to Him and the parents.
rows.anchor: ليذكر الولد بإحسانها المتقدم إليه

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muʿādh, sent by the Prophet, tells his hearers to worship God, avoid shirk, obey the Messenger for their good, and recognize that their final destination is everlasting Paradise or Hell.
rows.anchor: أن تعبدوا الله ولا تشركوا به شيئا، وأن تطيعوني لا آلوكم خيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman tells his son to establish prayer with its limits, duties, and times; enjoin good and forbid wrong as far as able; and endure the harm that such work inevitably brings.
rows.anchor: أقم الصلاة} أي: بحدودها وفروضها وأوقاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience through people's harm is one of the resolute affairs.
rows.anchor: إن الصبر على أذى الناس لمن عزم الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not turn your face away from people in contempt or pride; be gentle and meet them with an open face, as in the cited Prophetic advice.
rows.anchor: لا تعرض بوجهك عن الناس إذا كلمتهم أو كلموك، احتقارا منك لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the turned cheek as pride that belittles God's servants and turns away when they speak; al-ʿAwfī and ʿIkrimah also report this from him.
rows.anchor: وتعرض عنهم بوجهك إذا كلموك

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the phrase means speaking while turned away; Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, and several others are also cited with this interpretation.
rows.anchor: لا تكلم وأنت معرض. وكذا روي عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī interprets it as affected, side-mouthed speech, but Ibn Kathīr prefers the interpretation of turning away in pride.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم النخعي: يعني بذلك: التشديق في الكلام. والصواب القول الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿr is a disease that twists a camel's neck or head; the metaphor compares it to a proud person, and Ibn Kathīr quotes lines from ʿAmr ibn Ḥayy and Abū Ṭālib as evidence.
rows.anchor: وأصل الصعر: داء يأخذ الإبل في أعناقها أو رؤوسها

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: Luqman tells his son that wisdom can seat the poor among kings.
rows.anchor: يا بني، إن الحكمة أجلست المساكين مجالس الملوك

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: Luqman advises greeting people at a gathering, sitting quietly until they speak, joining if they remember God, and leaving if their talk turns elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ثم اجلس في ناحيتهم، فلا تنطق حتى تراهم قد نطقوا

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: Luqman illustrates the force of his advice by taking one mustard seed from a bag with each admonition until the bag is empty; the mountain would have split from the counsel, and his son did so.
rows.anchor: لقد وعظتك موعظة لو وعظها جبل لتفطر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet names Luqman, the Negus, and Bilal among three distinguished Black figures; al-Ṭabarānī explains that Abyssinians are meant.
rows.anchor: قال أبو القاسم الطبراني: أراد الحبش

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report says a poor man in two worn garments may pass unrecognized at people's doors, yet if he swears by God, God fulfills his oath.
rows.anchor: رب أشعث ذي طمرين يصفح عن أبواب الناس

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report calls the pious wealthy who are unnoticed when present and unmissed when absent lamps purified from every dark, disgraceful trial.
rows.anchor: طوبى للأتقياء الأثرياء الذين إذا حضروا لم يعرفوا، وإذا غابوا لم يفتقدوا

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muʿādh tells ʿUmar that even slight showing off is shirk and that God loves discreet, pious, wealthy people who are lamps of guidance and escape dark trials.
rows.anchor: إن اليسير من الرياء شرك، وإن الله يحب الأتقياء الأخفياء الأثرياء

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The Prophet says an unregarded man in worn clothes may have his oath fulfilled by God; if he asks for Paradise, God gives it, though He gives him nothing of worldly status.
rows.anchor: لو قال: اللهم إني أسألك الجنة لأعطاه الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says some Muslims are ignored by people if they ask for money but granted Paradise if they ask God; God neither gives them worldly goods nor withholds them because He despises them.
rows.anchor: لم يعطه إياها، ولم يمنعها إياه لهوانه عليه
